London, 24<sup>th</sup> February 2009 



# **Norilsk Nickel Daily News Digest** 

**Lonmin** announced that agreements regarding the retrenchment of employees at Marikana and Limpopo have been reached with trade unions.  Up to 4000 full time employees and contract workers at Marikana would lose their jobs.  Further, the miner agreed with trade unions that about 1 500 full-time employees at the Baobab shaft, Limpopo, would be retrenched, in line with the company’s plans to put the shaft on care-and-maintenance as soon as possible.  The company expects platinum sales for the 2009 financial year to be 0.7Moz, down 25 koz from 2008 sales, as a result of placing the Baobab shaft on care-andmaintenance. _Source:  Mining Weekly_ 

**Daimler** is open to any third party interested in its 19.9 % Chrysler stake and is unlikely to buy back its shares in the medium term.  A spokesman for Daimler said the company is currently negotiating only with Cerberus “and with no one else”, and that share buybacks were not on the table.  The Daimler CFO also said production cuts in the first half should help reduce bloated inventories and bring in some 3-4 billion euros ($3.8-$5.1 billion) in cash currently tied up in working capital. _Source:  Automotive News_ 

**Fiat SpA** ratings were cut into speculative, or “junk” status by Moody’s Investors Service, who said that the outlook for the company remains bleak.  The agency cut Fiat’s long-term rating by one notch to “Ba1,” the first level of junk. The outlook is negative.  Moody’s is expecting the automotive market to remain weak in 2009 and sees little chance of a meaningful rebound in 2010.  Moody’s is expecting car and light commercial vehicle demand to fall about 20 % in Q109. It is also expecting volume and cash flow to improve in the next few quarters. 

**Nissan Motor Co.’s** international credit rating fell a notch today because of concerns over the company’s declining cash flow.  Standard & Poor’s Ratings Services lowered Nissan’s long-term corporate credit and senior unsecured debt ratings to BBB from BBB+.  Nissan CEO Carlos Ghosn said this month that the automaker will lose about $2.9 billion in the 2008 fiscal year, which ends March 31. The automaker is cutting global costs in response, including the elimination of 20,000 jobs. _Source:  Automotive News_ 

**General Motors’ South Korean unit** may temporarily halt productions at two of its plants next month. GM Daewoo’s January sales slumped more than 50 % to 45,842 vehicles. The unit is holding discussions with Korea Development Bank, its main creditor, to boost finances. Still, GM Daewoo has no short-term liquidity problems, it said. The carmaker has exhausted a $2 billion credit line, according to the lender. GM also plans to halt work for several days at three of its plants in Mexico during March and April. _Source:  Bloomberg_ 

**Toyota, Honda** and other Japanese carmakers may post at least a combined 20% drop in February local sales, the Japan Aut

omobile Dealers Association said.  Japan’s vehicle sales, excluding minicars, plunged 28% last month, the biggest monthly drop since May 1974.  Japan is headed for its worst postwar recession as factory output slumped an unprecedented 9.6% in December and unemployment surged. _Source:  Bloomberg_ 

**TFT-LCD panel makers** AU Optronics (AUO) and Chi Mei Optoelectronics (CMO) dismissed a media report that said they were holding merger talks.  But AUO and CMO said that they will keep an open mind for possible partnership opportunities as long as they are good for the industry’s overall development. _Source:  Digitimes_
